node.label: Kimberlé W. Crenshaw
node.date_label: Race, Reform, and Retrenchment (1988) · Demarginalizing (1989) · Mapping the Margins (1991) · Critical Race Theory, co-edited (1995) · Toward a Field, coauthored (2013)
node.description: Kimberlé W. Crenshaw argues that treating race and sex discrimination separately obscures Black women’s subordination. “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989) names intersectionality as a way to expose that failure in law, feminist theory and antiracist politics. “Mapping the Margins” (1991) extends the approach to violence against women of color. Her legal framework became a resource across disciplines, including history, as she describes in a 2019 interview. It also prompted disagreement about how an analytical metaphor should travel: Jennifer C. Nash’s “On Difficulty” (2010) criticizes later scholarship that treats intersectionality as a settled truth or assumes that adding more intersections will overcome exclusion. Nash advocates retaining Crenshaw’s traffic analogy as one metaphor for investigating power. Crenshaw’s contribution belongs within an earlier and continuing Black feminist conversation, including the particular resources she takes from bell hooks and Gerda Lerner’s documentary collection.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “Race, Reform, and Retrenchment” (1988); “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989); “Mapping the Margins” (1991); Critical Race Theory: The Key Writings That Formed the Movement (1995), co-edited with Neil Gotanda, Gary Peller and Kendall Thomas; “Toward a Field of Intersectionality Studies” (2013), with Sumi Cho and Leslie McCall.
node.scope_note: Selected 1989 primary passages read in the publisher-hosted Chicago Unbound PDF: pp. 139–141, 153–160 and 166–167. “Mapping the Margins” was not read on a permitted route. Nash pages 1–2 and selected page 3, Higginbotham 2017 selected pp. 628–629, 633 n4 and 640, and UCLA interview answers read. Books, cited historical originals and the 1992 Hill chapter unread. The 2013 papers were read only as repository abstracts and metadata.

people_update.identity_note: Crenshaw explicitly locates her analysis as Black feminist in “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), subtitled “A Black Feminist Critique” (p. 139).

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), Crenshaw repeatedly cites hooks’s Ain’t I a Woman (1981), in notes 33, 38, 41 and 47, in discussions of Sojourner Truth, feminist exclusion, sexist imagery in Black liberation politics and racialized sexual stereotypes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the archived journal PDF, pp. 153–157: n. 33 cites hooks on Sojourner Truth; n. 38 cites her on exclusion from feminism; n. 41 on sexist imagery in Black liberation politics; n. 47 on sexual stereotypes. Visually checked printed p. 157: the hooks citation is in n. 47, not n. 46 as the finding recommends. These remain explanatory footnote citations rather than a named engagement with hooks in the body; hooks’s book unread. Retain the footnote-level warning and exclude this edge from the floor.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), Crenshaw develops intersectionality to explain Black women’s exclusion from single-axis antidiscrimination, feminist and antiracist frameworks.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary opening pp. 139–141 and conclusion p. 167 read; “single-axis framework.” Existing approach node and roster already recognize earlier Black feminist roots. This adds a direct person-to-approach route, not a new origin claim.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), Crenshaw argues that feminist theory evolves from a seldom-acknowledged white racial context, and shows through the separate-spheres literature how generalizations drawn from white women’s experience misdescribe the gender norms racism imposes on Black women and men.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex (1989), section II, printed pp. 154–155, in the archived journal PDF. The paragraph beginning The value of feminist theory explains its seldom-acknowledged white context; the following separate-spheres discussion shows how generalizations from white women’s experience obscure the simultaneous effects of racism and sexism on Black women and men. This supports a contribution to gender analysis through adjacent legal theory. No reading of Mapping the Margins (1991), no violence-specific argument, and no claim of adoption by all gender historians is asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: Speaking at UCLA in April 2026 about her memoir Backtalker (2026), Crenshaw placed it in the tradition of Black memoir and said she was “deeply influenced by Angela Davis and George Jackson”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UCLA Law news report (24 April 2026) of Crenshaw’s 16 April 2026 conversation with Cheryl Harris, section “On the narrative tradition in which Backtalker resides”, quoting Crenshaw: “I think it pulls from the tradition of Black memoirs – I was deeply influenced by Angela Davis and George Jackson, and the broad groups of folks who shaped our thinking.” This is a stated influence in Crenshaw’s own reported words, limited by its context to the Black memoir tradition. It makes no claim about Davis’s influence on Crenshaw’s legal theory. Neither Davis’s autobiography nor Backtalker was read. In “Demarginalizing” (1989), n. 42, Crenshaw also cites Davis’s Women, Race and Class (1981), but only as “See generally”, so that note is not used. The source is already in Crenshaw’s original packet as kc_w_backtalker_2026 (then used only for life status); it is reused here.
proposed_edges.map_label: Influenced by Davis’s Black memoir tradition

proposed_edges.relationship: In Intersectionality as Critical Social Theory (2019), Collins uses Cho, Crenshaw and McCall’s “Toward a Field of Intersectionality Studies” (2013) as a starting point for identifying intersectional thinking tools and framing her own questions about thinking, difference and power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed preview, chapter 1, p. 23: Collins explicitly takes the coauthors’ definition as a resource and develops questions from it. This credits joint intellectual work, not coauthorship between Collins and Crenshaw. The 2013 article body is unread; its repository record confirms metadata. This differs from held kc_w_04 and phc_w_05.
proposed_edges.map_label: Starting point for intersectional thinking tools

proposed_edges.relationship: In her essay on protected beliefs and employment tribunals (2024), Sara Ahmed applies Crenshaw’s analysis in King was a critical race theorist before there was a name for it (2022) to attacks on antiracist work in Britain.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Author’s essay read. Ahmed quotes Crenshaw within her US–UK comparison, then applies the argument to Britain. The claim concerns this particular uptake, not Ahmed’s entire theoretical development or an independent assessment of tribunal law.
proposed_edges.map_label: Applies Crenshaw’s account of anti-CRT attacks
